title: Should We Encourage Lame Duck Colleagues to Stick Around?
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article questions the common practice of keeping departing colleagues around for extended transition periods. It argues that even well-liked departing employees can unintentionally erode team morale simply by their prolonged physical presence, since their discontent tends to leak out even unintentionally. The piece recommends a short, clearly bounded transition window and suggests removing lame-duck colleagues from meetings and day-to-day interactions as quickly as possible. It closes by urging leaders to treat departing colleagues gracefully while still protecting the morale of those who remain.
points: Questions the value of prolonged transition periods for departing colleagues
Explains how a lingering departure can unintentionally undermine team morale
Recommends a short, clearly bounded exit window rather than an extended one
Balances graceful treatment of leavers against protecting remaining team morale
quotes: For a host of reasons, colleagues sometimes decide to move on to greener pastures.
When physically present for more than a few days, even the best leavers can subtly undermine the confidence and morale of their prior teammates.
There is little upside in allowing lame duck colleagues to hang around.
The sooner they disappear, the faster others can focus on the tasks at hand.
Leaders can take the high road and treat leavers gracefully without ignoring the negative influence their presence will have on others.
Lame duck colleagues serve best away from the table. Duck sauce, anyone?
